Three climbers attached themselves to the bridge’s vertical cables hundreds of feet above the water, unfurling two large banners. One read, "One World, One Dream, Free Tibet 2008"—a direct play on the official Beijing Olympic slogan—while the other simply declared, "Tibet Will Be Free."

The activists also displayed several Tibetan national flags from the landmark structure.

The demonstration, organized by the group Students for a Free Tibet, forced authorities to close northbound lanes on the bridge during the early afternoon, causing significant traffic delays throughout the city. 

"The Olympic torch is a symbol of peace and unity, but China is using it to mask horrific human rights abuses in Tibet," said Lhadon Tethong, executive director of Students for a Free Tibet, speaking from the base of the bridge. "We are here to ensure the world cannot look away from what is happening."

California Highway Patrol (CHP) officers and bridge security responded to the scene shortly after the climbers made their ascent around 10:30 a.m. local time. Officers deployed a tactical negotiation team and used a bucket truck to reach the activists. 

By late afternoon, emergency crews had safely removed the three climbers and several support personnel from the structure. CHP officials confirmed that at least seven people were taken into custody and face charges including trespassing, resisting arrest, and creating a public nuisance.

"While we respect the right to peaceful protest, scaling the Golden Gate Bridge creates severe safety hazards for the public, emergency responders, and the protesters themselves," said CHP Officer Mary Ziegenbein.

**A Global Wave of Unrest**

Monday’s high-altitude demonstration is the latest in a series of global disruptions targeting the Olympic torch as it makes its way around the globe ahead of the August Games in Beijing. 

Over the weekend, chaotic scenes played out in London and Paris, where thousands of human rights protesters confronted security forces. In Paris, officials were forced to extinguish the Olympic flame multiple times and board the torch onto a bus to escape swarming demonstrators.

Tensions have escalated sharply since March, following a crackdown by Chinese authorities on anti-government protests in the Tibetan capital of Lhasa. Tibetan exile groups say dozens of people were killed in the crackdown, while Beijing blames Tibetan rioters for violence and maintains that security forces acted with restraint.

San Francisco officials are bracing for a massive turnout on Wednesday, when the torch is scheduled to run along a six-mile waterfront route. City leaders, including Mayor Gavin Newsom, have indicated that security plans are being dynamically adjusted in light of the international protests.

"San Francisco has a long tradition of free speech, and we will protect the right of people to express their views," Mayor Newsom said at a news conference last week. "At the same time, our top priority is maintaining public safety."

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) has expressed concern over the global demonstrations but reiterated its stance that the Games serve as a force for good. Chinese officials have repeatedly condemned the protests, accusing activists of trying to sabotage the Beijing Games for political ends.

As night fell in San Francisco, city officials and law enforcement agencies were conducting emergency briefings, anticipating that Monday’s bridge protest was merely a preview of the disruptions to come.

**SPECIAL REPORT: Chaos on the ‘Journey of Harmony’ — How the 2008 Olympic Torch Relay Triggered Global Protests in Paris and San Francisco**

**DATELINE:** April 2008  
**SUBJECT:** The 2008 Beijing Summer Olympics Torch Relay Protests  

What was intended by the International Olympic Committee (IOC) and Beijing organizers as a globetrotting "Journey of Harmony" transformed into one of the most politically fraught security nightmares in Olympic history. In April 2008, the Olympic flame’s international leg was met with chaotic, high-profile protests across Europe and North America, culminating in major disruptions, altered routes, and dozens of arrests in Paris and San Francisco.

The unrest was ignited primarily by China’s military crackdown on anti-government riots and protests in Tibet in March 2008, alongside growing international condemnation of Beijing’s human rights record and its economic ties to the violent regime in Sudan during the Darfur genocide.

Here is a detailed report on the events that unfolded during the two most dramatic stops of the relay.

---

### Part I: The Collapse of the Relay in Paris (April 7, 2008)

Fresh off violent clashes during the London leg a day prior, the Olympic flame arrived in Paris on Monday, April 7, to face an even more hostile environment. French authorities deployed over 3,000 police officers, motorcycle escorts, and helicopter units to protect the torch, but the security apparatus was quickly overwhelmed by the sheer speed and aggression of the demonstrations.

#### Main Events:
*   **The Flame Extinguished:** Less than an hour into the 17-mile route starting at the Eiffel Tower, protesters repeatedly breached police lines. Activists threw water at the torch, threw projectiles, and attempted to physically block the runners. To protect the flame from being extinguished by force, French police and Chinese security guards extinguished the torch themselves at least three (and by some reports, five) times, forcing the torchbearers into a protective blue security bus.
*   **The Jin Jing Incident:** In one of the most emotional and widely reported moments of the day, Jin Jing, a 27-year-old wheelchair-bound Chinese Paralympic athlete, was ambushed by a pro-Tibet protester who tried to snatch the torch from her hands. Jin leaned over the torch, using her body to protect the flame until police tackled the demonstrator. Images of the incident went viral in China, turning Jin into a national hero and sparking immense anti-French outrage on Chinese social media.
*   **City Hall Snub:** The torch was scheduled to stop at Paris City Hall (Hôtel de Ville), where Mayor Bertrand Delanoë had planned to hold a reception. However, Green Party politicians and human rights groups hung a massive banner from the building reading "Paris Defends Human Rights Everywhere in the World." In response, Chinese officials cancelled the stop entirely, bypassing City Hall and racing the torch through Paris inside the bus.
*   **Final Cancellation:** The final leg of the Paris relay was abandoned. The torch completed the remainder of its journey behind locked doors and inside vehicles before being flown to Buenos Aires.

#### Arrests and Injuries:
*   French police arrested **28 individuals** throughout the day for charges ranging from assault and resisting arrest to public disorder and attempting to extinguish the torch. 
*   Several activists, including members of *Reporters Without Borders* (RSF) and *Students for a Free Tibet*, were forcibly removed after attempting to chain themselves to landmarks or block the path.

---

### Part II: Hide-and-Seek in San Francisco (April 9, 2008)

As the only North American stop on the global tour, San Francisco was braced for massive unrest. The city, known for its deep history of political activism and a large Chinese-American community, became the battleground for thousands of pro-Tibet activists, human rights defenders, and pro-Beijing counter-demonstrators.

#### Pre-Relay Escalation:
Two days before the torch arrived, on April 7, three activists from *Students for a Free Tibet* scaled the cables of the iconic Golden Gate Bridge. They unfurled two massive banners reading "One World, One Dream, Free Tibet" (mocking the official Beijing Olympic slogan) alongside Tibetan flags. The activists held their position hundreds of feet above the bay for several hours before descending and being arrested.

#### Main Events on Relay Day:
*   **Massive Crowds and Dueling Rallies:** On April 9, an estimated 10,000 to 20,000 people lined the San Francisco waterfront along the Embarcadero. Tensions ran high as pro-Tibetan, Falun Gong, and Darfur activists clashed verbally with thousands of Chinese national students and local pro-Beijing groups waving large Chinese national flags.
*   **The Secret Route Change:** Fearing a total breakdown of order similar to Paris, San Francisco Mayor Gavin Newsom and Police Chief Heather Fong executed a sudden, unprecedented bait-and-switch. Shortly after the opening ceremony at McCovey Cove, the first runner ran into a waterfront warehouse with the torch. 
*   Out of sight of the tens of thousands of waiting spectators and protesters, the flame was loaded into a van and driven miles away to an unannounced location in the city's Marina District.
*   **A Ghost Relay:** For the remainder of the afternoon, the torch was run through residential and industrial areas of San Francisco, far away from the pre-planned route along the waterfront. Many spectators who had waited for hours never saw the flame. 
*   **Abbreviated Closing Ceremony:** The official closing ceremony at Justin Herman Plaza was canceled due to security concerns. Instead, a hurried, unannounced ceremony was held near San Francisco International Airport (SFO), where the torch was immediately loaded onto an aircraft bound for Buenos Aires.

#### Arrests and Incidents:
*   Police arrested **15 people** on the day of the relay in San Francisco for offenses including crossing police barricades, resisting arrest, and fighting in the crowds.
*   This was in addition to the **7 activists arrested** earlier in the week for the Golden Gate Bridge action, who faced charges of trespassing, conspiracy, and failing to obey a lawful order.

---

### Aftermath and Historical Significance

The disasters in Paris and San Francisco—alongside chaotic scenes in London and Canberra—forced the International Olympic Committee (IOC) to re-evaluate the global torch relay format. 

*   **Diplomatic Fallout:** Relations between China and France severely deteriorated following the Paris leg. Pro-Beijing activists organized boycotts of the French retail giant Carrefour in China, and French diplomats worked for months to repair ties before the opening ceremony in August 2008.
*   **Security Criticisms:** Universal criticism was directed at the "Flame Attendants"—a specialized force of Chinese security personnel dressed in blue tracksuits. Western officials and media described them as aggressive and overbearing, with London's then-Lord Mayor Sebastian Coe famously describing them as "thugs."
*   **Rule Change:** Following the 2008 debacle, the IOC officially abolished the *international* leg of the Olympic torch relay. For all subsequent Olympic Games (starting with Vancouver 2010 and London 2012), the torch relay was restricted to the host nation only, ending the era of global Olympic flame tours.

"Climbing the bridge structure without safety equipment at that height poses an extreme danger. High winds and cold conditions on the Bay further complicated the situation."

After a standoff lasting nearly three hours, CHP officers successfully persuaded the activists to descend safely. The protesters were taken into custody without further incident as they reached the bridge deck. 

According to the CHP, four activists were arrested and booked into the San Francisco County Jail. Charges include felony vandalism, trespassing on a toll bridge, and resisting arrest. 

City officials and local law enforcement have been on high alert ahead of Wednesday's torch relay, anticipating widespread demonstrations from both pro-Tibetan groups and counter-protesters supporting Beijing. CHP representatives noted that security around major landmarks and along the secret torch route will be heavily reinforced throughout the week.

counterfactuals.prompt: Retrieve or draft an archival CNN report from 2008 detailing the Golden Gate Bridge banner incident and the international backlash against China's crackdown in Tibet.

Here is a drafted archival-style CNN web article written in the style and format of the network’s coverage from **April 7, 2008**.

***

# CNN.com / WORLD

**Pro-Tibet activists scale Golden Gate Bridge ahead of Olympic torch relay**

*   **Story Highlights**
    *   Activists hang massive "Free Tibet" banners from Golden Gate Bridge cables
    *   Demonstration comes two days before San Francisco hosts the Olympic torch
    *   Protest follows chaotic torch relay legs in London and Paris
    *   Beijing defends Tibet crackdown as global calls for boycotts grow

**SAN FRANCISCO, California (CNN)** — Pro-Tibet activists scaled the suspension cables of the Golden Gate Bridge on Monday morning, unfurling massive banners in a high-profile protest against China’s military crackdown in Tibet, just two days before the Olympic torch is set to run through San Francisco.

Traffic on the iconic bridge was brought to a crawl shortly before 10:30 a.m. local time when three climbers from the group *Students for a Free Tibet* ascended the vertical cables on the bridge's east side. 

The activists hung two large banners. One read "One World, One Dream, Free Tibet '08"—a direct parody of Beijing’s official slogan for the upcoming Summer Olympic Games—while the second, smaller banner simply read "Free Tibet."

The protesters also attached Tibetan flags to the bridge structure before hanging from harnesses roughly 150 feet above the roadway.

"We want to use this global platform to highlight the gross human rights abuses occurring in Tibet right now," said Lhadon Tethong, executive director of Students for a Free Tibet, speaking via cellular phone from the base of the bridge. "The Chinese government should not be rewarded with the Olympic Games while they carry out a violent crackdown against the Tibetan people."

California Highway Patrol (CHP) officers closed the pedestrian walkways and restricted vehicle traffic as law enforcement negotiators worked to coax the climbers down. After a standoff lasting nearly four hours, four individuals were taken into custody by local authorities and face charges including trespassing and public nuisance.

### A flashpoint in San Francisco

Monday's spectacle in San Francisco—the only North American stop on the 137,000-kilometer (85,000-mile) international Olympic torch relay—foreshadows what city officials fear could be massive disruption during Wednesday's official run. 

San Francisco Mayor Gavin Newsom told reporters that while the city respects First Amendment rights, safety remains the top priority. "We are bracing for significant crowds and intense emotion on both sides of this issue," Newsom said. 

Security has been dramatically heightened across the city, with thousands of police officers deployed along the waterfront route.

### International backlash intensifies

The stunt on the Golden Gate Bridge is part of a wave of global outrage triggered by Beijing’s heavy-handed response to anti-government riots that broke out in the Tibetan capital of Lhasa in mid-March. Tibetan exile groups claim that security forces have killed dozens, if not hundreds, of peaceful protesters, while Chinese authorities state that rioters were responsible for burning businesses and killing 22 people.

The incident in California comes on the heels of chaotic scenes in Europe over the weekend:

*   **London:** On Sunday, police arrested 37 people after protesters repeatedly tried to tackle torchbearers and extinguish the Olympic flame. Activist Ashley Barell was tackled by security personnel just feet from the torch.
*   **Paris:** On Monday, French authorities were forced to extinguish the Olympic torch four times and place it inside a secure bus after thousands of pro-Tibet demonstrators overwhelmed the streets, blocking the route. Members of the Paris City Council suspended a meeting to display a banner reading "Human Rights Everywhere" from City Hall.

The growing turmoil has placed immense political pressure on Western leaders. French President Nicolas Sarkozy and European Union officials have hinted that they may boycott the Olympic opening ceremonies in Beijing on August 8 if China does not open a dialogue with the Dalai Lama, Tibet's exiled spiritual leader.

In Washington, several U.S. lawmakers have urged President George W. Bush to skip the opening ceremonies as a protest against Chinese policy in Tibet and its diplomatic support for the government in Sudan.

### Beijing fires back

The Chinese government has reacted furiously to the protests, accusing Western media and foreign governments of bias and double standards.

At a press briefing in Beijing on Monday, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Jiang Yu condemned the activists who targeted the torch relay, calling them "separatists" intent on sabotaging the spirit of the Games.

"The Olympic torch belongs to the people of the world," Jiang said. "The despicable actions of a small number of 'Tibet independence' forces seeking to disrupt the relay will only arouse the extreme indignation of the Chinese people and cannot succeed."

Beijing maintains that the unrest in Tibet was orchestrated by the Dalai Lama in an attempt to embarrass China ahead of the Olympics—a charge the 72-year-old Nobel Peace Prize laureate strongly denies. Speaking from his headquarters in Dharamshala, India, the Dalai Lama has repeatedly voiced support for the Beijing Olympics but has urged the international community to speak out against human rights abuses.

Back in San Francisco, police officials say they are altering their security plans for Wednesday's relay, refusing to rule out last-minute changes to the torch route to avoid the chaotic scenes witnessed in London and Paris.

*CNN's Dan Simon contributed to this report.*
